supremeCourt.name: Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación (SCJN)
supremeCourt.appointmentMethod: As of the 2024 reform, justices are ELECTED by popular vote (previously: nominated by the President, confirmed by the Senate).
supremeCourt.fspEraChanges: Landmark change: the 2024 judicial reform (promulgated Sept 2024 under AMLO, championed by Sheinbaum) makes ALL judges — including the Supreme Court — elected by popular vote, cuts the SCJN from 11 to 9 justices, and shortens tenure from 15 to 12 years. The first judicial elections were held 1 June 2025 and a newly elected court was seated in Sept 2025. Critics (Mexican Bar, HRW, scholars) warn it undermines judicial independence; supporters say it democratises the judiciary.
supremeCourt.stillServing: The pre-reform court was effectively replaced. An entirely new 9-justice court was elected on 1 June 2025 and seated 1 September 2025 (12-year terms), with Hugo Aguilar Ortiz as chief justice (2025–2027). Three former AMLO-appointed justices (Lenia Batres, Yasmín Esquivel, Loretta Ortiz) were re-elected. Turnout was about 13%, and the new court is widely assessed as aligned with the ruling Morena party.

courtHistory.event: The SCJN was re-founded by the 1917 Constitution; under PRI hegemony it was repeatedly resized and was effectively subordinate to the executive.

Zedillo's judicial reform reduced the SCJN from 26 to 11 ministers (early-retiring the sitting court), created the Federal Judiciary Council (CJF), and set 15-year staggered terms — building the modern, more independent court.
Morena's judicial reform (promulgated Sept 2024 under AMLO) made all judges elected by popular vote, cut the SCJN from 11 to 9, and shortened tenure from 15 to 12 years.

The first judicial elections (1 June 2025) replaced the entire court; the new 9-justice SCJN seated 1 Sept 2025 is widely assessed as Morena-aligned — critics call it a capture of the court by popular-vote means.

benchControl.note: The SCJN was appointed entirely under PRI and PAN governments; Zedillo's 1994 reform cut the court from 26 to 11 ministers on 15-year staggered terms. Morena first took the presidency in December 2018.

AMLO's nominations seated Juan Luis González Alcántara (Dec 2018), Yasmín Esquivel and Margarita Ríos Farjat (2019) and Loretta Ortiz (2021) — 4 of the 11 seats by 2021 — with Lenia Batres (Jan 2024) the fifth after Zaldívar's resignation.

Under the Morena-designed 2024 reform the entire court was replaced by popular election (1 June 2025, roughly 13% turnout); observers assess all nine justices seated in September 2025 as aligned with or backed by Morena — supporters call the reform democratisation, critics the loss of a check on the ruling party.

justices.name: Hugo Aguilar Ortiz
justices.background: Indigenous-rights lawyer; topped the 2025 judicial election.

supremeCourt.justicesNote: Top 4 of the 9 elected justices; the remaining 5 are still to be added (see #45).

fspParties.note: Mexico's FSP members are MORENA (which joined around 2015 and led the 2018 turn to power), the Partido del Trabajo (PT), and the older Partido de la Revolución Democrática (PRD) — the party Andrés Manuel López Obrador belonged to before founding MORENA. By 2024 the PRD had collapsed: it ran with the PAN/PRI-led opposition, won a single deputy, and lost its national registration. In government MORENA and the PT sit together; the coalition's supermajority relied on the non-FSP Partido Verde (PVEM).

legislativeControl.seats: The FSP-aligned left (the PRD from 1989, the PT from 1990) sat in opposition to the PRI and then PAN governments; the PRD was at times the third-largest force and governed Mexico City, but never won the presidency or a congressional majority.

López Obrador's MORENA won the 2018 presidency and, with the PT and the non-FSP PVEM, majorities in both chambers; the 2024 election under Claudia Sheinbaum returned a two-thirds supermajority in the Chamber of Deputies and a near-supermajority in the Senate.

government.note: MORENA and the PT — both FSP members — together hold 287 of 500 seats, a majority in their own right. The full 'Sigamos Haciendo Historia' coalition (adding the non-FSP PVEM, 364 seats) reached the two-thirds supermajority needed to amend the constitution without the opposition. Note the historically FSP-listed PRD ran with the opposition here and won a single seat before losing its registration.

MORENA and the PT hold 68 of 128 Senate seats — a majority on their own. The coalition (with PVEM, 82 seats) fell a few seats short of a two-thirds supermajority at the election and reached it only through later defections.
